To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the use of simplified hip joint geometry (e.g. spherical or conchoid) and a smoothed cartilage surface can grossly overestimate contact pressures and underestimate contact area; and 2) the assumption of rigid bones in FE models of hip joint cartilage mechanics can lead to large overpredictions in contact pressures.

simplifications of the hip joint geometry and material properties can significantly alter the predicted cartilage contact pressures and that a subject-specific FE model with deformable bone is necessary for accurate predictions of cartilage mechanics in the hip.

simplifications to hip joint geometry and material properties can have dramatic effects on predictions of hip joint contact stresses and that the use of deformable bones in finite element models of the hip may be necessary for accurate prediction of cartilage contact stress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a computational model to predict the effects of joint geometry and loading conditions on cartilage contact stress in the hip.
the development and evaluation of a subject-specific finite element model for the human hip joint.

the effects of joint geometry on finite-element predictions of hip cartilage stress, and how these predictions can be used to elucidate the role of cartilage mechanics and joint morphology in the development of osteoarthritis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

simplifications of hip joint geometry and material properties may be sufficient for the purpose of studying the effects of joint morphology on cartilage mechanics and the relationship between cartilage mechanics and hip osteoarthritis, but not sufficient for predicting the magnitude and distribution of hip joint contact pressures.

the simplifications to the model geometry, cartilage surface, and bone material properties used in the present study have a dramatic effect in the prediction of the magnitude and distribution of the cartilage stresses in the hip joint.
the simplification of geometry, cartilage surface, and bone material properties will lead to underestimation of contact stresses in the articular cartilage of the hip joint.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hip joint is a complex structure with a non-spherical geometry, and it is important to consider this in biomechanical analyses.
a subject-specific model with a realistic representation of bone geometry and a smooth cartilage surface is required for accurate predictions of cartilage stresses in the hip joint.
the geometry of the hip joint and the material properties of the bone-cartilege interface are very important to consider when modeling hip joint biomechanics.
The main takeaway from our work is that

simplifying the geometry of the hip joint may be acceptable for certain applications (e.g., modeling the effects of hip morphology on cartilage mechanics) but not for others (e.g., estimating cartilage contact stress in the hip joint).
subject-specific models are necessary to accurately predict contact stresses in the human hip.
the hip is a very complex joint and that it is important to consider the effects of joint geometry and cartilage mechanics when modeling hip joint mechanics.
